name: Eclipse Glacium
specific_features: Permanent eclipse shadow from orbiting debris cloud
description: Eclipse Glacium is permanently shrouded by a dense debris cloud in close orbit, the remnants of a shattered moon that now cast a perpetual partial eclipse across the ice-bound surface. The reduced stellar input has locked the planet in a deep freeze, its surface covered in glacier sheets that extend from pole to pole without interruption. Beneath this frozen shell, a liquid ocean persists, heated by the planet's residual internal warmth, and cryovolcanic geysers periodically breach the surface in spectacular eruptions of water vapor and ice crystals.

The thin atmosphere carries a constant haze of ice particles expelled by the cryovolcanoes, creating a sparkling mist that catches what little starlight penetrates the debris cloud. The light on the surface is perpetually dim, a twilight that never deepens to full darkness nor brightens to true day. Ice tectonic ridges mark where glacier sheets collide and thrust upward, creating mountain ranges of pure ice that groan and crack with glacial movement.

Microbial life has been confirmed in the subsurface ocean, supported by chemosynthetic processes around hydrothermal vents on the ocean floor. These organisms exist in complete isolation from the surface, their ecosystem entirely self-contained within the dark waters beneath kilometers of ice. The discovery prompted a reassessment of life's requirements, demonstrating that stellar energy is not necessary when geological energy suffices.

Eclipse Glacium's subsurface ocean is the target of a major astrobiology research program, with drilling stations established at three locations on the ice sheet. The drilling operations must proceed slowly to avoid contaminating the pristine ocean below. The orbiting debris cloud complicates access, requiring navigational precision to thread the approach corridors that have been mapped through the densest concentrations of fragments.
